Ohio property tax is assessed by the county auditor, and owners can file a valuation complaint with the county Board of Revision. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A valuation complaint for the current tax year is filed with the county auditor on or before March 31 of the ensuing tax year or the closing date of first-half collection, whichever is later. (ORC 5715.19(A)(1) (eff. Mar. 20, 2026); source)
  • For homestead reduction, 'sixty-five years of age or older' means a person who attained age 64 before Jan 1 of the application year; permanently and totally disabled defined by impairment on Jan 1 of application year or agency certification. (ORC 323.151(B), (D); source)
  • The ORC 319.302 partial exemption (non-business-credit rollback) as amended (latest legislation HB 186, 136th GA; version eff. Mar. 20, 2026) provides 10% for farming property and, for residential property, 7.5% for the first tax year the amendment applies, with cumulative 2.5-point reductions in each of the following two years and 0% thereafter. The older flat '2.5% rollback' for owner-occupied residential should NOT be stated as current. (ORC 319.302(B) (excerpt only; full text and applicability dates not seen); source)
  • CAUV 'land devoted exclusively to agricultural use' includes parcels under 10 acres with average yearly gross income of at least $2,500 over the three prior years (or anticipated), and commercial agricultural uses (eff. Mar. 20, 2026 version). (ORC 5713.30(A)(2); source)
  • County prosecuting attorney institutes foreclosure of the state's tax lien in the treasurer's name upon delivery of a delinquent land tax certificate or master list, in a court or the county board of revision (ORC 323.66); prosecuted like mortgage foreclosure; publication three consecutive weeks if by publication. (ORC 5721.18 (eff. Oct. 3, 2023); source)
  • Any person entitled to redeem delinquent land may do so before filing of the entry of confirmation of sale (or before expiry of the alternative redemption period under 323.78) by tendering taxes, assessments, penalties, interest, charges and costs to the county treasurer. (ORC 5721.25 (eff. Apr. 7, 2009); excerpt partial; source)
  • 'Tax certificate' under 5721.30 is a document (physical, book-entry or electronic) at the treasurer's discretion and is distinct from the delinquent land tax certificate under 5721.13; 'certificate parcel' means the delinquent land described in a tax certificate. (ORC 5721.30(A)-(B) (eff. Nov. 2, 2018); source)

  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Ohio disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

  • Court examines the sale and, if proper, within 30 days of return of the writ journalizes satisfaction and orders title transferred to purchaser (confirmation). (ORC 2329.31(A) (eff. Sept. 29, 2017); source)
